newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-GOLOTA SAYS IT BEST WHEN HE CALLS HIMSELF STUPID.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-GOLOTA SAYS IT BEST WHEN HE CALLS HIMSELF STUPID.

text.p: "I stupid. I stupid. I stupid."
No one can argue with Andrew Golota about that. It's a refrain he often punctuates with slaps to his own head when he makes mistakes, according to his co-trainer, Lou Duva.

No one can argue with the slaps either. And on Sunday, no one could argue with anyone who might wait on a long line of people applying for the job of administering corporal punishment to the Polish fighter for wilfull stupidity.

It can be assumed that even the fighter's mother wouldn't argue against her son -- disqualified on Saturday for repeated low blows against Riddick Bowe for the second time in five months -- having those words carved into his forehead for daily reference, especially if he hopes to fight again.

Golota, who once again was ahead on all three judges' scorecards going into the ninth round when he was disqualified, is a fighter only Sigmund Freud could love. And Freud is probably the only one who could begin to understand the 28-year-old fighter's insistence on self-destruction.

Golota was handily beating Bowe, even after having two points deducted, one each for a head butt in the second round and one after a low blow in the fourth round, following repeated warnings from referee Eddie Cotton. Throughout the scheduled 10-round fight, Golota was landing far more and much harder punches than Bowe, who was only a shell of the fighter who had twice captured the heavyweight championship of the world.

Bowe, who had ballooned to some 280 pounds (127 kg) by September, lost at least 45 pounds (20 kg) in what seemed have been his cornermen mistaking scrawny for svelte. The weight loss appeared to leave Bowe, 29, weak and at times standing on memory alone. Often Bowe's exhaustion left him stumbling around the ring at the Atlantic City Convention Centre like a rank amateur after missing with wild swings.
Golota twice knocked Bowe down -- in the second round and again in the fifth round.

But Bowe, whose three battles with Evander Holyfield are classics of recent years, displayed a champion's heart by not going down for good from Golota's onslaughts, and was able to recall enough remnants of his championhip talent to knock down Golota for the first time in his career with a whirlwind of punches in the fourth round.
Golota, though, got up quickly. But he almost immediately continued throwing very low blows, for which he was warned.

"When he realises things are not going his way, he resorts to hitting low, head butts," said Bowe after the fight. "He was a stong, game guy. Unfortunately, he just started hitting low. That's because he got somewhat winded and he didnt know how to react."
Finally, Bowe went down in the fourth round after one of the low blows. The referee took a point away, and Bowe took about a minute of the five minutes permitted to recover.

In their first fight on July 11 in Madison Square Garden, Bowe, understandably, could been accused of some method acting in his portrayal of pain from the low blows. But on Saturday in Atlantic City the repeated low blows seemed to have caused genuine pain.
By the ninth round, Golota seemed just a round away from catapaulting himself into the top ranks of heavyweights with accompanying major paydays.
Duva said he told his fighter in the later rounds to throw only straight punches to the head and not to go to the body.

But true to his strange form, Golota, who in previous fights had bitten an opponent on the shoulder and head butted another, took aim at Bowe's nether region, sending Bowe down with several punches to the protective cup.
The referee moved in quickly and with a disgusted look on his face waved off the fight at 2:58 of the ninth round.

"He was warned, and I took away a point for a head butt earlier, and I took another point away for a low blow that was really blatant and then the third low blow, and that's a disqualification," said referee Cotton.
Bowe, now 40-1, gave conflicting impressions of whether he will continue to fight, which is not unusual for a fighter after a particularly tough fight.
But Bowe said, "I hope someday Mr Holyfield gives me another opportunity."
Holyfield, of course, stunned the boxing world last month by ike Tyson to win the World Boxing Association title.
Duva said he would sit down with Golota, now 28-2, to determine whether his fighter wants to be a professional fighter "or the heavyweight champion at a bar."
"He's an intelligent guy," Duva said, adding that he does not know, "what makes him have those instincts to go low."
After Saturday, it would seem to stretch credibility to put "intelligent" and Golota in the same sentence.
